app_asset_retriever_note: Not on the list, and worth naming because docs/memory-ownership.md section 4 used to claim it was: AppAssetRetriever.h:15 declares a TemporaryHost property and AppAssetManager.m:59 assigns it beside the app, so the asynchronous box-art path (AppAssetRetriever.m:29 reads app.host.uuid through boxArtPathForApp:) already holds its host. Section 5 step 3 is therefore already done for that path, and the two holders above are the whole of what step 2 and step 3 still owe.

app_assignment_sites.AppsViewController.m|item.app: configureItem: hands an AppCell its app and nothing else. AppCell.h:20 stores the app and declares no host, and AppCell.m:129 reads self.app.host.uuid to look up the artwork dimming for that host. Harmless while the back-pointer is strong -- the app is what keeps the host alive, which is the first observation of this experiment -- and a nil read in a collection view the moment it is not. This is section 5 step 3's shape, in the apps page rather than in the artwork queue.
app_assignment_sites.AppsViewController.m|streamVC.app: prepareForSegue: hands a stream its app and nothing else (AppsViewController.m:613). StreamViewController.h:25 declares the app and no host property, and StreamViewController+Diagnostics.m reads self.app.host across the stream's diagnostics, including the address it writes and the settings buckets it reads. Today the stream's host is alive because the stream's own app is holding it.

app_assignment_sites_note: The keys are `file|holder.app` rather than line numbers, because line numbers move and a record that has to be edited every time a file above it gains a line stops being a record. The record is the set of holders that lean on the strong back-pointer, and it is only read while `app.host` is strong: the day it turns weak the same rule refuses any site still on this list, which is why the list cannot be quietly widened and cannot be quietly dropped.
filed_record_refusals_note: One entry per record filed in `scripts`, keyed by file name, and the value is the list of refusals that file must draw. `ownership-sample.json` is the run of 2026-09-25 on this laptop after the reap landed: one host in the library, none of them the probe's, the reap keeping them, and the shapes unchanged from the run before it -- so it has to draw nothing. `ownership-sample-prereap.json` is run 36019606141, filed a day earlier: the CI runner's reading, whose library was the memory sweep's leftover, and it must draw the refusal naming the field that run's build could not have recorded. The red team also fills that field in and requires the older record to go green, which is what makes the refusal a verdict about the reap rather than a coincidence of shape. `ownership-sample-cleaned.json` is the run that pressed `ML_PROBE_REMOVE_OWN_HOSTS` on this laptop: two hosts found, one of them the seed's, that one removed through the app's own deletion path and the other left standing -- `removed-some`, which is the one reap status a human sets rather than a job. Expectations move when records arrive, which keeps relaxing a rule and filing a record two different edits. `ownership-sample-cleaned.json` predates the app-record counting, so it must draw the refusal for a deletion whose rows were never counted -- and the red team fills the count in from the seed's own fan-out and requires it to go green, so the refusal stays about the missing evidence. `ownership-sample-cascade.json` is the run that answered the Core Data question: a planted host was removed and its three app records went with it (six rows before, three after, none of them orphaned), so the model's `Cascade` is a measurement and not a grep. Records filed before ML_PROBE_PARTIAL_HOST_INFO existed are expected to be refused for that absence and for nothing else: filled in, they go green again. The four older records gained two more refusals each on 2026-09-25, and no rule was relaxed to admit them: the run that measured the two holder shapes is what makes a record from before it incomplete, so `ownership-sample.json` -- re-filed from that run -- is the one record that now draws nothing, and the repair that fills the two shapes back in is what proves the older records are refused for the absence rather than for their library, their reap, or their date.
library_sharing: One database per machine, not one per probe. `DatabaseSingleton` resolves its store under `NSApplicationSupportDirectory` in `NSUserDomainMask`, which comes out of the account record and not out of `$HOME`, so a Debug probe started with a private temporary home still opens the same SQLite file as the app a person uses. Measured, not inferred: an empty temporary `HOME`, a probe asked to seed one host, and a report of the laptop's own two hosts. Every probe in this repository had assumed the opposite, and one of them was deleting the directory it believed it had written to. What follows from it: the steps of one CI job share a library, and a run that measures `the library` without asking who put hosts in it may be measuring the previous run. `ML_PROBE_REAP_OWN_HOSTS` and `probeOwnedHosts` are what turns that from an assumption into a reading.

observed.app_asset_retriever_correction: docs/memory-ownership.md section 4 recorded the box-art path as a holder with no host. It has one: AppAssetRetriever.h:15 declares a TemporaryHost property and AppAssetManager.m:59 assigns it beside retriever.app, so the asynchronous boxArtPathForApp: read of app.host.uuid is over a host the request itself is holding. Section 5 step 3 is therefore already done for that path, and the two sites above are the whole of what steps 2 and 3 still owe.

ci_runner.correction_seed_status: WRONG IN THE FIRST FILING, corrected from the run's own log. This block used to say both arches reported seed status `seeded`. The first ownership print appeared in run 36019606141 and both arches read `1 host(s) in the library, seed status existing-hosts`. The `seeded` had been carried over from the memory sweep's line in the same job, which does seed a host: the sweep runs a step earlier, and the probe that came to measure a graph it would plant itself found the sweep's host already in the database. Two readings of two steps had been merged into one record, which is the mistake this file exists to make expensive.
ci_runner.measured_on: 2026-09-25, run 36029410301, GitHub macOS runners, arm64 and x86_64, word for word alike: 1 host in the library and 1 of them planted by a probe, the reap reporting `reaped`, the seed then reporting `seeded`, and the three shapes reading as they had on the laptop -- production appList 3 and both objects alive with nobody holding them, hand-built the same at appList 1, and the lone back-pointer going back. This is the first ownership run on a runner that measured a graph it made itself.
ci_runner.seeded_then_existing_in_one_job: The memory sweep prints its own seed status three times in one job and they are not all the same line: `seeded`, then `existing-hosts` twice. That is the shared library again rather than a change of shape -- the first sweep of the pair plants the host and the sweeps after it find what the first one wrote. The growth judgement compares two sweeps over that one library, which is what it wants; what is no longer allowed anywhere is a reading that calls such a leftover `somebody's library` without saying so, which is why the ownership probe now reaps first and prints whose host it measured.
ci_runner.what_still_needs_a_thing_we_do_not_have: a live stream session. The runners judge the object graph and the assignments; nobody has yet watched a running stream read `app.host`, and the holder rule is a guarantee about the source until somebody does.
ci_runner.what_the_runners_add: The seed path, genuinely this time. A runner has nothing to discover, so the graph it measures is one a probe wrote through the production `DataManager` -- and, since the reap, the graph the ownership probe wrote and not the one the sweep left. The laptop reaches the same table through `existing-hosts` over a real library, which is the point: the reading does not depend on whose LAN answered, and it no longer depends on which step ran first.

laptop.measured_on: 2026-09-25, one Debug probe build on this laptop, after the reap: one host in the library, none of them planted by a probe, the reap recording `kept` and leaving it alone, and the three shapes reading exactly as they did the day before -- which is the check that the reap changed who holds what and not what is held
laptop.what_the_cleanup_found: Before the reap there were two hosts in this library, and the first run of the reap called the library mixed: one of the two carried the seed's uuid prefix. An earlier sweep had planted it here while believing the temporary `HOME` it was handed kept it out of the machine's own store. It was removed through the app's own `removeHost:` under `ML_PROBE_REMOVE_OWN_HOSTS`, the flag a person sets for their own machine; the default reap still refuses a mixed library, because it cannot tell a leftover from somebody's GameStream host and guessing deletes a machine from somebody's list. The host that remains is the one this laptop streams to.

observed.unpaired_sites_found: prepareForSegue: (AppsViewController.m:613, the stream) and configureItem: (AppsViewController.m:724, the AppCell, which reads self.app.host.uuid at AppCell.m:129). Both are alive today because the app is what keeps the host alive, which is the first observation of this experiment rather than an inference.
observed.what_the_controls_are_for: handBuiltGraph exists only to agree with productionGraph: if the two disagree, something outside the pair is holding it and no reading in the report describes the app. backpointerOnly has nothing pointing back at the app, so it is required to go back; if it survives, the probe is holding the objects it claims to watch and the leak in the other two shapes is the harness's. Both controls are refused rather than warned about, because they are the only reason the third reading means anything.
observed.what_this_does_not_measure: the stream's own holder. StreamViewController stores an app and declares no host (StreamViewController.h:25), and this experiment builds no view controller, so nothing here can watch a live stream read app.host. That half is judged off the tree by the holder rule in scripts/ownership-audit.py -- every statement that hands an app to a holder has to give that holder a host too, refused outright under a weak back-pointer and refused as a new entry while the back-pointer is still strong -- and the two halves together are what section 5 of docs/memory-ownership.md asked for before ownership could change.

app.host=strong,host.appList=strong.name: shipped today: the cycle is present, and every holder leans on the strong back-pointer

app.host=weak,host.appList=strong.name: after the section 5 fix: the cycle is gone, and no holder keeps a host alive by holding its app alone

shape_contract.why: the counts are the definition of the shapes, not a property of the library. A hand-built graph with no app pointing back is the third shape wearing the second shape's name, and the agreement between the two graphs -- the control that says nothing outside the pair is retaining it -- would then be an agreement between two copies of the same shape. The holder shapes carry no `appListCount`, because the host is not reachable from the holder through the graph they are defined by: what makes one of them the shape it names is what the holder was given, so `holderKind` is its definition and a paired holder reporting itself app-only is the same quiet swap as a hand-built graph with no app pointing back.

holder_shapes.name: The two shapes that watch a holder which is not the app, and the difference between them -- the pairing's contribution, measured on 2026-09-25 instead of argued off the header.
holder_shapes.measured_on: 2026-09-25, the same Debug probe build and the same library as the `laptop` record below, in the same run: five shapes, one process, and the three graph readings unchanged from the run before them.
holder_shapes.what_the_difference_says: Both shapes build the graph the way `-[TemporaryHost initFromHost:]` leaves it, both cut the back-pointer by hand (`app.host = nil`), and both then let the probe's own references go, so the holder outside the graph is the only hand left on the pair. The holder given the app alone lost the host; the holder given the app and the host kept it. That gap is the whole of step 2 and step 3 of section 5: a holder that is handed its host by name does keep it, and a holder that is not loses it. Until today this was read out of `App.h` and `Host.h`; it is now a number, and it is the number the fix has to reproduce when the declaration changes.
holder_shapes.what_the_controls_prove: Both holders died when the probe dropped them (`holderAliveWithNoHolder` false in both), which is what makes the two readings belong to the holder rather than to the harness. The pair died with them in both shapes, so nothing in the process outlived the last holder. A harness that leaked here would make the paired shape's `yes` meaningless, which is why the audit refuses the control rather than warning about it.
holder_shapes.why_it_does_not_depend_on_the_declaratio: The shapes sever the edge themselves, so the reading is the contribution of that edge held fixed, not a prediction about a future build. That is also why both profiles in `profiles` expect the same readings from them: a fixer who flips `app.host` to weak and finds these numbers unchanged has confirmed the pairing does the job, and one who edits the expectation instead has edited the experiment.
holder_shapes.what_this_still_does_not_measure: A live stream session. The probe constructs no `StreamViewController` and no `AppCell`, and the session's own references are in no process this run can see, so these shapes say what a holder that is given a host is worth and nothing about whether every holder in the app will be given one. The holder rule read off the tree is what judges the second half, and it refuses an unpaired holder under a weak back-pointer outright.
